Management Plan
2026
Directorate-General for European Civil
Protection and Humanitarian Aid
Operations
1

PART 1. Introduction
Strategic planning and programming is the cornerstone of the Commission’s performance
management framework, as outlined in the Commission’s strategic plan for 2025-2029. This
multi-annual strategic plan provides a basis for annual planning and reporting by the
departments on their main objectives and achievements. It also offers an umbrella under which
each department presents their strategic outlook for the current mandate of the Commission,
as set in the Political Guidelines 2024-2029.
The mission statement, operating context, 2025-2029 strategic outlook and efforts to
contribute to cross-cutting Commission priorities related to the implementation and
simplification agenda (1) remains unchanged, as outlined in DG ECHO’s strategic outlook in the
Management plan 2025.
Part 2 of the management plan provides the main outputs that DG ECHO plans to deliver on the
Commission Priorities 2024-2029 in 2026. Part 3 defines the main outputs that DG ECHO plans
to deliver on common multi-annual objectives to build a modern and sustainable public
administration in 2026.
The related outputs with their indicators and targets are shown in Annexes 1 and 2 to this plan.
The chart below illustrates how the general objectives, specific objectives and key performance
indicators reflect the core aspects of DG ECHO’s performance.
(1) See Communication A Simpler and Faster Europe
3

PART 2. Delivering on the Commission’s
priorities in 2026
The mission of the Directorate-General for European Civil Protection and Humanitarian
Aid Operations (DG ECHO) is to help save and preserve life, prevent and alleviate human
suffering and safeguard the integrity and human dignity of populations affected by natural
hazards and human-induced disasters. To that end, DG ECHO acts both as the EU
humanitarian aid donor and emergency responder as well as a coordinator and facilitator of
civil protection operations through the Union Civil Protection Mechanism (UCPM). This is a
fundamental expression of the European value of solidarity.
Nowhere is DG ECHO’s dual mission as present as in Ukraine. Russia’s war of aggression
against Ukraine continues to cause civilian deaths and suffering, massive displacement, and
large-scale destruction of infrastructure. According to the 2025 UN Humanitarian Response
Plan, 12.7 million people in Ukraine will need humanitarian assistance. The Commission will
continue providing substantive humanitarian aid to help civilians affected by the war and
will continue implementing the largest civil protection response operation in the history of
the UCPM. Civil protection support focuses on emergency response capacities, energy and
health sectors including the coordination of medical evacuations of Ukrainian patients in urgent
need of treatment. DG ECHO’s humanitarian intervention focuses on emergency first-line
response to the most vulnerable. DG ECHO will also continue its assistance to Ukrainian
refugees in Moldova (around 70,000 people), while facilitating their integration into the
national social protection systems, under a Humanitarian-Development-Peace Nexus approach.
Moreover, the Commission supports Ukraine and Moldova in enhancing their capacities in the
field of civil protection and their further integration into the UCPM.
Communication
DG ECHO will continue its efforts to increase awareness, understanding of and support for
the EU’s work on humanitarian aid and civil protection in 2026. DG ECHO’s communication
actions will continue to evolve and adapt, explore new digital platforms and help counteract the
spread of misinformation. This will be achieved through a steady digital presence, ad hoc
technical press briefings, collaborations with established media partners (e.g. podcasters,
content creators and traditional journalists). Integrated campaigns on EU humanitarian aid
(#VoicesOfHumanity) and on EU civil protection preparedness operations will aim to reach
over 30 million Europeans across EU countries. A citizen panel on population preparedness,
co-organised with DG COMM, DG EAC, DG SANTE and DG HERA will take place in Spring 2026,
with the participation of 150 randomly chosen EU citizens, one third of which under 30 years
old. In November 2026, DG ECHO will organise the 9th Civil Protection forum and under the
Preparedness Union Strategy, DG ECHO will also deliver, in collaboration with Member States,
key population preparedness actions to foster a culture of preparedness and risk awareness.
4

General Objective 2: A new era for European
defence and security
Specific Objective 1: The EU is prepared to anticipate and manage all hazards and
their cascading effects.
DG ECHO is and will continue to be leading on the development and implementation of several
of the EU Preparedness Union Strategy’s key actions in 2026 (PUS). These include
developing a comprehensive EU risk and threat assessment, adopting EU minimum
preparedness requirements, developing guidelines to reach population self-sufficiency of
minimum of 72 hours. In March, marking the one-year anniversary of the PUS, DG ECHO will
host a Preparedness Conference to showcase first deliverables and progress of the PUS and to
discuss the next steps and actions with stakeholders. Furthermore, in co-lead with DG EMPL, DG
ECHO will organise a Social Partners Preparedness Summit. Moreover, it will foster the use and
integration of the Copernicus Emergency Management Service (CEMS); adopt guidelines for the
“stress-testing” of emergency response and crisis centres and increase awareness about risks
and threats. DG ECHO will also work on developing guidelines for Member States to increase
risk communication as well as guidelines on how to act in emergencies, tailored to all types of
disabilities (sensorial, physical and intellectual). Jointly with DG EAC, DG ECHO is also
developing preparedness actions related to youth and education. DG ECHO will conduct regular
EU-level exercises to promote comprehensive preparedness (including those involving NATO)
together with SG.
In 2026, rescEU capacities will be further increased. Firstly, DG ECHO will implement the
procurement of rescEU medium amphibious planes, including the recent grants for two new
helicopters awarded in 2025. In parallel, forest fighting capacities will be maintained at the
level of ambition set out in the rescEU transition arrangements.
Concerning other rescEU capacities, the focus will be on finalising the procurement of medical
and Chemical, Biological, Radiological and Nuclear (CBRN) items, while maintaining existing
capacities available for deployment and making sure that projects concerning medical
(Emergency Medical Teams and Medevac) and CBRN (Detection and Decontamination) teams
become gradually operational. Further, DG ECHO will actively engage with DG HOME and other
relevant services to prepare a new CBRN Preparedness and Response Action Plan, an
action under the ProtectEU Strategy, to revise the 2017 Action Plan to enhance preparedness
against CBRN security risks.
Concerning Emergency Medical Teams (EMTs), the work to ensure the availability of the first
operational capacities with specialised care teams (EMT-2 project) will continue in 2026. The
Medical Evacuation Capacity (MEDEVAC) whose scope was extended to burns and CBRN
patients, will continue and another MEDEVAC asset will be available in the latter half of 2026.
Shelter and energy supply reserves will be developed further. The multi-purpose transport
and logistics capacity, operational since September 2025, will support relevant civil protection
operations via the use of the relevant planes.
In complementarity to the development of rescEU capacities, continued focus will remain on the
European Civil Protection Pool (ECPP). As the key UCPM pillar for deploying capacities, DG
5

ECHO will dedicate efforts throughout 2026 to strengthen the ECPP, by engaging with Member
States and Participating States (MS/PS) in co-funding the upgrade or repair of response
capacities, certifying already committed capacities and re-certifying capacities as necessary.
In 2026, the Emergency Response Coordination Centre (ERCC) will further develop actions
towards effective civil-military interactions. It will notably convene meetings and workshops
with Member States with regards to establishing comprehensive civil–military preparedness
arrangements. Further, the ERCC will conduct the EU Integrated Resolve 2026 exercise,
coordinating the Commission’s participation, together with the EEAS and the General Secretariat
of the Council, under a renewed EU–NATO Parallel and Coordinated Exercise (PACE)
Concept. The exercise will test the Commission’s internal crisis coordination mechanisms,
aiming to strengthen inter-institutional cooperation during crises as well as to increase
engagement with NATO.
The Union Civil Protection Knowledge Network will continue supporting activities aimed at
preventing and preparing for disasters. Key priorities for 2026 will be to foster the work of its
capacity development- and science pillars and further consolidate cross-cutting knowledge
management activities. Under the Capacity Development Pillar, DG ECHO manages annual
grants for prevention and preparedness activities including both single- and multi country
grants to national authorities of UCPM Member States, Participating States (2), to carry out
improvement of crisis management capabilities, including full-scale exercises, development of
studies, preparation of reforms, improvement of early warning tools, and more. DG ECHO also
manages a peer review programme at national and sub-national level, with two peer review
reports to be published in 2026. Under the Science Pillar, DG ECHO will further support
innovation and notably the identification and uptake of technologies from the Horizon Europe
research programme, such as on artificial intelligence for preparedness. Supporting national
authorities to integrate innovation related to Disaster Risk Management will continue to be a
priority through UCPM calls for proposals (KAPP).
In line with the EU Preparedness Union Strategy, DG ECHO will promote the integration of
preparedness by design into key EU policies, legislation, and programmes, with a focus on
mapping EU funding sources for long-term investments in disaster risk management and crisis
preparedness from several policy areas. In addition to mapping funding sources, dialogue with
relevant authorities from Member States could also look at bottlenecks and capacity gaps to
access and implement investment funding. DG ECHO will continue supporting Member States
to improve wildfire risk management though dedicated peer reviews, upon request. Following
the devastating 2025 wildfire season, DG ECHO will steer developments to improve the early
warning and information system for wildfires. Further, DG ECHO will actively engage with DG
ENV and other relevant services to explore options through a dedicated Communication to step
up efforts for integrated wildfire risk management.
To improve EU’s civil protection and crisis response, DG ECHO, together with DG HERA, has
proposed the Regulation on the Union Protection Mechanism and Health Emergency
Preparedness and Response (UCPM/HER Regulation) on which negotiations with the co-
(2) Prevention and preparedness are funded through several grants with different eligibilities. The
KAPP Grant: UCPM MS, PS, Neighbourhood, IPA countries are eligible for the KAPP grant and
UCPM MS PS, and Kosovo are eligible for Track 1 and TAFF grants.
6

legislators are expected to continue throughout 2026. The new Regulation merges for the first
time UCPM with health emergency response actions, in line with the ambition of the Niinistö
Report and the Preparedness Union Strategy to boost the Union’s capacity to deal with all
aspects of crises. It aims to simplify procedures for key actions such as setup of logistical and
medical hubs, evacuations, and using private sector donations. It also seeks to adjust co-
financing rates and streamline rescEU deployments outside the EU by focusing on Union-level
impact as well as on broader disasters of significant international concern. To improve clarity, a
separate annex will list actions eligible for Union financial support, removing them from the
Regulation’s main body.
In this context, DG ECHO will work towards establishing progressively the EU Crisis
Coordination Hub by 2027 subject to the outcome of the negotiations on the UCPM/HER
Regulation. The Hub will build on the structure and expertise of the ERCC, including its
analytical and scientific capabilities, situational awareness, and 24/7 operational capacity for
cross-sectoral crises. The objective of the Hub is to continue and further upscale support to
Member States in managing the cross-sectoral consequences of crises, based on reinforced
planning and more comprehensive analysis.
General Objective 4: Sustaining our quality of
life: food security, water and nature
Specific Objective 1: The needs of people in times of crises are met.
Whenever disaster strikes, any affected country inside or outside the EU can request
assistance from the UCPM through the ERCC. In 2026, the ERCC will continue to effectively
coordinate Member States and Participating States, the private sector, and other services to
continue providing relief assistance to populations affected by disasters and vulnerable
communities.
The UCPM is, through its external dimension, an instrument enabling EU solidarity in the
world. The number of activation requests from third countries, approximately three quarters of
all requests, and the increasing diversity and comprehensiveness of assistance provided,
demonstrates its growing importance. DG ECHO will continue to foster this type of cooperation
to support third countries in the aftermath of a disaster. UCPM actions will be implemented in
line with the Preparedness Union Strategy and the Disaster Resilience Goals (DRGs).
To support response, DG ECHO is committed to strengthening the ERCC’s ability to access and
utilise scientific, analytical, monitoring, information management, and communication
resources, thereby enabling more informed, timely, and evidence-based decision-making. In
2026, DG ECHO will continue to collaborate with the Joint Research centre (JRC), with DG DEFIS
and other relevant Commission services as well as the EEAS and agencies to further develop
these capabilities. These collaborations will contribute to the provision of comprehensive
situational awareness including in sensitive situations for example through Copernicus
Emergency Management service and Copernicus Support to EU External and Security Actions.
7

To improve emergency management and disaster response in Europe and beyond, DG ECHO
plans to establish a Scientific and Technical Advisory Facility (STAF). STAF is envisaged as
a toolbox available to the ERCC and Member States, designed to bring together and organise
the analytical and scientific capacities developed by the European Commission under various
programmes, such as the EU Space Programme (including Copernicus) and the UCPM,
within a single, coherent framework. In this vein, DG ECHO will establish in 2026 a new
partnership providing 24/7 expert assessment on the consequences of conflicts. STAF will
further strengthen the ERCC and support the future EU Crisis Coordination.
Specific Objective 2: EU Humanitarian aid and civil protection operations are
equipped to prepare and respond to the adverse effects of climate change
As the climate and environmental crisis deepens, humanitarian actors are faced with a
collective responsibility to ensure that their work does not contribute to further deteriorating
the environment. DG ECHO will continue acting as a leading donor on the greening of
humanitarian aid. To reduce the carbon footprint and the environmental damage of
humanitarian aid, DG ECHO will continue the implementation of the minimum environmental
requirements and associated guidance and explore the feasibility of increasing the level of
ambition of the requirements in line with the outcomes of the evaluation expected in 2026.
Risk-informed disaster preparedness is part of the overall objective of providing relief and
support to the most vulnerable people affected by natural hazards and human-induced crises
across the world by mobilising both humanitarian aid and European civil protection assistance.
In 2026, DG ECHO will continue to implement its approach to disaster preparedness, which
promotes multi-hazard preparedness and anticipatory action. Improvements on supply
chain preparedness will continue to be supported to build local supply chain capacity and
assess opportunities for local procurement of goods and services. DG ECHO will monitor and
facilitate the integration of preparedness measures and climate, environmental and conflict risk
considerations into all the humanitarian actions it funds to ensure that climate related impacts
are accounted for in all interventions.
General Objective 6: A global Europe: Leveraging
our power and partnerships
Specific Objective 1: The EU remains a leading humanitarian donor by providing
effective humanitarian assistance to the most vulnerable.
DG ECHO provides principled and needs-based humanitarian aid around the world. Providing
rapid and flexible assistance both in major crises and in forgotten crises has become a
hallmark of the EU's profile as a donor, especially as confronted with major challenges, e.g. the
unprecedented global funding gap, challenges to the UN system and multilateralism, and rising
violations of International Humanitarian Law.
DG ECHO will uphold its efforts in 2026 to ensure delivery of humanitarian aid even when
access to affected people is severely restricted, and assistance is delivered despite volatile and
8

insecure circumstances. Moreover, DG ECHO works with other donors and stakeholders to
promote a principled approach and a coherent way to address humanitarian needs.
In 2026, with 295 million people (3) identified as being acutely food insecure globally, DG ECHO
will continue providing support on food security to those most in need. To that end, DG
ECHO will promote the broad application of its new Humanitarian Food and Livelihood
Assistance (HFLA) policy with a preference for cash (versus in-kind) as a delivery modality.
In terms of health, in 2026 DG ECHO will foster a cross-sectoral approach to health and in
particular integrated health-nutrition interventions, health preparedness, sexual and
reproductive health, and mainstreaming mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) in
humanitarian response. DG ECHO will launch a renewed application and maintenance process
for Humanitarian Procurement Centres (HPCs), particularly key for medical procurement. Finally,
DG ECHO will continue to contribute to the implementation of the EU Global Health Strategy.
An estimated 234 million children globally are in need of access to education (5). DG ECHO will
sustain its strong commitment to Education in Emergencies actions worldwide, maintaining
investment in education at the level of 10% of the initial EU humanitarian aid budget,
prioritising projects targeting at least 50% of girls. Throughout interventions, DG ECHO will
ensure that beneficiaries have access to safe drinking water and sanitation (WASH).
Given the ever-increasing needs and limited resources, aid effectiveness and result-oriented
actions will remain a priority. DG ECHO will continue its work on commitments taken under the
Grand Bargain10, notably on flexible, multi-year funding, localisation (by implementing DG
ECHO’s localisation guidance and progressing toward the target of 25% of funding reaching
local actors), coordinated and impartial needs assessment, and simplification of reporting.
In 2024 DG ECHO launched the Humanitarian Leaders Group on Supply Chain which
culminated at a high-level conference held in December 2025, after a year of intensive dialogue
and joint work across the humanitarian community. Discussions underscored the urgency of
continuing the process of transformation of supply chains to meet rising humanitarian needs in
the context of constrained financial resources. In 2026, the objective is to start the
implementation by a gradual move from fragmented, individual approaches towards a
collaborative, cross-cutting humanitarian supply chain network. This will include driving efficiency
and value by fostering collaboration between field-based actors, the UN and INGO’s, further
embedding environmental sustainability into humanitarian operations, fostering an interoperable
digital ecosystem for enhanced efficiency and transparency, empowering local actors through
equitable partnerships and securing long-term investments through flexible and inclusive funding
models.
Examples of humanitarian crises to which DG ECHO will respond in 2026
In line with its mandate, DG ECHO will continue to provide needs-based humanitarian
assistance in crises around the world and to respond to the most urgent and acute needs of
affected populations. In 2026, along with Ukraine, focus will be put on the major crises outlined
below:
(3) Global Report on Food Crises 2025 September Update
9

The humanitarian situation in Palestine remains dire more than two years into the conflict. The
entire 2.1 million population in Gaza is facing high levels of acute food insecurity and is in
need of humanitarian assistance. Approximately 81% of all structures in the Gaza Strip are
damaged. Additionally, the West Bank has been marred by unprecedented levels of violence,
deepening food insecurity and heightened protection risks.
Over 16.5 million people in Syria, as well as Syrian refugees and vulnerable host communities
in neighbouring countries (Türkiye, Lebanon, Jordan, Egypt and Iraq) will continue to receive
humanitarian assistance.
An estimated 22.9 million people need humanitarian assistance in Afghanistan, including
returnees, with approximately 9.5 million people experiencing high levels of acute food
insecurity in the period May-October. The Afghanistan crisis is compounded by forced returns of
Afghans from neighbouring countries, notably Iran and Pakistan. In 2025 alone, 2.3 million
Afghans have been forced to return to Afghanistan.
The humanitarian situation continues to deteriorate dramatically in Sudan as a consequence of
the war that broke out in 2023. The scale of the crisis is unmatched with record high food
insecurity, including famine conditions, as well as widespread international humanitarian law
(IHL) violations and massive protection needs. Sudan is the largest child displacement crisis in
the world, with over 5 million children displaced inside and outside the country. About 30.4
million people, including 16 million children (4), were in need of humanitarian aid and protection
in 2025. That number is expected to further increase in 2026.
The conflict in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) took a drastic turn at the
beginning of 2025 when the M23 group, supported by the Rwandan Defence Forces conquered
large parts of North and South Kivu, including their capitals Goma and Bukavu where ECHO
offices are located. Despite ongoing peace initiatives and the signing of a peace agreement, the
conflict keeps raging, with new displacements, epidemics outbreaks and, particularly, escalating
levels of sexual- and gender-based violence. A total of 19.9 million people are estimated to be
in need of humanitarian assistance.
The Central Sahel region (Burkina Faso, Mali, Niger) and Central Africa (Nigeria, Chad,
Central African Republic and Cameroon) experience a proliferation of security incidents and
community conflicts. Humanitarian access remains challenging, and the situation is forecasted
to deteriorate in 2026 as non-state armed groups are increasing their attacks and the flow of
refugees crossing the border from Burkina Faso to Mali onwards to Mauritania is sustained. The
total number of people in need of food assistance is estimated to increase up to 55 million,
with over 1 million children severely malnourished in Nigeria alone. The regions report wide IHL
violations and face challenges such as access constraints including aid criminalisation/
misperception of the role of humanitarian actors, bureaucratic and logistical impediments.
The Greater Horn of Africa countries (Ethiopia, Somalia, Kenya, Djibouti, South Sudan and
Uganda) are affected by increasing humanitarian needs due to conflicts, epidemics and natural
disasters. 18.8 million people in Ethiopia, 9.3 million people in South Sudan) 5.9 million people
(4) Sudan: Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan 2025.
10

in Somalia, 2.28 million people in Uganda and 3.7 million people in Kenya are in of need
humanitarian assistance in 2025.
The Southern Africa and Indian Ocean region is vulnerable to climate change, natural
hazards, conflicts and epidemics. Three tropical cyclones hit the region between December
2024 and March 2025. Some 20 million people in the region face acute food insecurity. The
surge in violent non-state armed groups in Northern Mozambique has forced 168 000 people
to flee between July and October 2025.
In Southeast Asia, two regional complex crises have root causes in Myanmar: the Rohingya
regional refugee crisis, broken out in 2017, and the 2021 internal conflict in Myanmar. In 2025,
about 22 million people have been in need of humanitarian assistance in Myanmar, including
3.6 million IDPs. Over 1.15 million Rohingya refugees live in the largest refugee camp in the
world in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh, entirely dependent on humanitarian assistance. Furthermore,
the region is extremely vulnerable to natural hazards. In the Philippines, for instance, typhoons,
floods and earthquakes affected over 17 million people in 2025.
In Venezuela, the humanitarian situation is severe for 19.6 million people. Following the US
large scale military operation in early January 2026 leading to the removal of the Venezuelan
President, the country has entered a new, possibly volatile, transition phase. This development
could add significant uncertainty and complexity to an already fragile humanitarian situation.
This in a country with soaring inflation rates, from which over 7.8 million people have already
left. The situation may lead to deteriorating humanitarian needs and deepening protection risks
both in the short and medium term as well as causing spill-over effects in the region.
In Haiti, six million people are in need of humanitarian assistance. 90% of the metropolitan
area of the capital Port au Prince is under the control of gangs with consequent high exposure
to extortions, kidnappings, killings, and gender-based violence. More than 1.3 million have been
displaced by the crisis, mostly women and children.
DG ECHO will continue to respond to humanitarian needs arising from unexpected crises
(natural and /or human-induced, including outbreaks of epidemics). This will be done through
ReliefEU Funding. To complement the EU’s role as a donor, DG ECHO also intervenes in direct
operations. The objective of ReliefEU Capacities is to facilitate the quick delivery of
humanitarian assistance. They will be further developed in 2026, by expanding the scope and
coverage of already existing capacities (i.e. stockpiles; etc.) and by creating new capacities in
new sectors such as health and water access, sanitation and hygiene (WaSH).
Specific Objective 2: Humanitarian space is preserved and respect for
International Humanitarian Law is ensured
In 2026, DG ECHO will prepare a Communication on Humanitarian Aid, as announced in the
Commission Work Programme for the same year. In light of the evolving geopolitical landscape,
the growing complexity of crises and the stark funding gap, the Communication will reaffirm
the EU’s commitment to principled humanitarian action. It will set out the EU’s actions to: a)
enhancing the humanitarian space and strengthening humanitarian diplomacy; b) improving
performance of the system such as the humanitarian supply chain, and c) looking for effective
partnerships to address root causes of fragility and increase resilience, including through
developing an integrated approach to fragility.
11

Considering the dramatic disrespect for International Humanitarian Law (IHL) in today’s
armed conflicts, with a direct impact on the surge of humanitarian needs, in 2026 DG ECHO will
focus on boosting humanitarian diplomacy efforts in support of IHL and humanitarian
access. DG ECHO will carry out systematic public advocacy and will continue coordination on
these efforts. DG ECHO will also make funding available for supporting compliance with IHL by,
among others, supporting prevention of violations, monitoring compliance and protecting aid
workers. On humanitarian access, DG ECHO will continue to strengthen its policy framework by
integrating field insights and expertise on armed actors with policy guidance and advocacy.
Further, DG ECHO will continue promoting and supporting the compliance of EU sanctions,
counterterrorism, and counterterrorism financing measures with IHL. To that effect, DG ECHO
will, as appropriate, promote the consistent inclusion of standing humanitarian exceptions,
including humanitarian exemptions in line with UN Security Council Resolution 2664 (2022).
The centrality of protection in humanitarian action and focus on the most vulnerable remain
paramount, given that protection risks are often at the heart of humanitarian needs. This also
extends to the protection of humanitarian personnel, who increasingly operate in high-risk
environments. DG ECHO remains committed to gender-and age and disability
mainstreaming, accounting for specific needs of those most at risk, and the multiple,
intersecting forms of discrimination.
Given the protracted nature of most humanitarian crises, improving and strengthening the link
between humanitarian and development aid, and, where relevant, peace actions, is
necessary to better connect urgent relief and longer-term solutions. In 2026, DG ECHO will
continue undertaking systematic EU joint analyses of the risks, and structural drivers of crises,
including contributing to conflict analysis screenings mandated by the Neighbourhood,
Development and International Cooperation Instrument (NDICI).
At strategic level, DG ECHO will work to ensure that the humanitarian narrative is an integral
part of the EU’s overall positioning in support of the global system of governance and the
rules-based international order. The EU and its Member States, working in a Team Europe
approach, will maintain their steadfast commitment to the multilateral humanitarian system. As
reliable, predictable and principled donor, DG ECHO, in coordination with EU Member States, will
remain at the forefront of steering an inclusive, sustainable and transformative Humanitarian
Reset, while ensuring coherence with the broader UN80 initiative.
Equally important, DG ECHO will press on with its dialogue with regional organisations and
international cooperation, such as the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), the African Union (AU)
or Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and pursue its specific dialogue on
humanitarian issues with the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS). An
Administrative Arrangement with the Indian National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) is
expected to be signed with India.
Finally, DG ECHO will contribute to the simplification agenda by following up on a number of
nascent internal simplification initiatives, such as simplify the certification process of NGOs,
increased use of standardised protocols in rescEU deployments and curbing top-ups for
protracted crises and enhancing ReliefEU. DG ECHO will also contribute to the 2026 Annual
12

Progress Report for Simplification, Implementation and Enforcement for Commissioner
Lahbib (ECHO-HERA-JUST) which will be coordinated by DG JUST and delivered in Q3.
13

PART 3. A modern and sustainable public
administration: outputs in 2026
The internal control framework supports sound management and decision-making. In particular,
it ensures that risks to the achievement of objectives are addressed and reduced to acceptable
levels through cost-effective controls.
DG ECHO has established an internal control system tailored to its particular characteristics and
circumstances. The effective functioning of this internal control system will be assessed on an
ongoing basis throughout the year and will be subject to an annual assessment covering all
internal control principles.
A. Human resource management
In a context of high workload, high turnover due to staff composition combined with limitation
of resources, DG ECHO HR focus will remain on the implementation of the HR strategy including
actions identified in DG ECHO’s local HR strategy, in close collaboration with the internal
communication unit.
DG ECHO remains committed to develop and engage with its staff in Headquarters, ECHO Field
Network and EU Delegations, building upon existing actions notably through the ECHO HR
Listening cell, the ECHOlistic workplace action (both stemming from the 2023 Biennial
corporate Staff Survey follow-up action plan of DG ECHO) and regular exchange between staff
and senior management. DG ECHO will build upon the results of 360° feedback mechanisms for
middle and senior managers launched early 2025, identifying the best tools to reinforce
interpersonal and leadership skills and further develop management proficiency.
DG ECHO stays committed contributing to the Commission strategy on Diversity and Inclusion,
notably by sustaining achievements in gender balance in management positions (in 12/2024 a
42% of middle managers were women. By 06/2025, this figure had increased to 44%. DG
ECHO aims to increase this rate to at least 50% by 2029), notably through the corporate
Management Development Programme, by supporting appointments of female managers and
coaching women in pre-management positions, expected numbers of participants are detailed
in Annex 2. DG ECHO will promote geographical balance in management and recruitments and
will also encourage mobility within the DG.
B. Digital transformation and data management
DG ECHO is committed to evolving its digital governance through a structured framework in line
with the corporate IT governance approach: The ECHO IT Steering Committee, chaired by the
Director General, sets the IT vision and strategy, prioritising investment and resource allocation.
User committees define functionalities, while steering committees guide project focus. DG
ECHO is committed to enhancing its digital environment and infrastructure and continue
harmonising the ECHO field infrastructure.
14

Throughout early 2025, 24% of statutory staff engaged in IT training. To enhance digital skills
and based on the Strategic Objective 1: Digital Culture, we propose targeted analysis and
frequent EU Learn consultations, emphasising AI tools. Cybersecurity awareness shows
progress, with clicking rates down by 15% and we will continue to further improve. We plan to
intensify briefings, organise roadshows, and engage with corporate CyberAware campaigns,
including dedicated campaigns for DG ECHO field office staff. Collaboration will pivot on locally
promoting tools like MS Teams and M365 through hands-on awareness sessions for HQ and
field offices staff. The expected outcome of these awareness sessions is detailed in Annex 2.
To advance Strategic Objective 2: Digital-ready Policymaking, we aim to maintain staff
capabilities through EU Learn resources and train policy officers on assessment of digital
impact. With 100% of policy initiatives reviewed for digital impacts so far in 2025, DG ECHO,
though rather operational than a policy DG, strongly emphasises digital inclusion.
In line with the Strategic Objective 3: Business-driven Digital Transformation, DG ECHO targets
further enhancing datasets on data.europa.eu. DG ECHO will continue optimising
interoperability, map data assets, and ensure quality checks. Innovation KPIs will be bolstered
by mapping needs, fostering synergies, and investing in AI. By collaborating on Commission-
wide initiatives and utilising AI solutions, we aim to drive digital advancement and foster agile
development practices. DG ECHO will further digitalise the core security process through the on-
going project Mission Security Clearance Tool (MSCT). A new module “Mission Security
Clearance” will be available in the Field Staff Management system (FSM) live in production
expected in Q1 2026
To achieve Strategic Objective 4, "Seamless Digital Environment", we will continue focussing on
modernising our IT systems, ensuring all information systems are properly mapped, and
identifying user needs before investing in new solutions. Where possible, we will also prioritise
cloud adoption, leverage open-source solutions and promote awareness on cloud infrastructure
services. In the area of crisis management, DG ECHO will continue the transformation workplan
for CECIS CP 2.0 following the revision of the implementing act, implement additional security
measures in line with the IT security plan and modernise CECIS MP reusing most of the
components of CECIS CP 2.0. Further, to facilitate and secure access to data and to improve
quality and avoid duplication, in 2026, DG ECHO will deploy the remaining dashboards (Civil
Protection Data Repository project) developed with the support of DIGIT for the EC Data
Platform.
To address Strategic Objective 5, "Green, secure and resilient infrastructure", we will promote
the Digital Workplace Portal and its informative resources to support staff needs. Building on
our above-average cybersecurity risk maturity, we will maintain up-to-date IT Security Plans
and collaborate closely with the DG DIGIT. Additionally, we will promote eco-friendly practices,
such as paperless operations and raise awareness about the energy consumption of AI
prompts. DG ECHO will continue increasing the level of cybersecurity of its information systems
and ECHO Field Network infrastructure by making use of the CERT-EU and DG DIGIT to perform
vulnerability and stress testing of new modules/applications.
Regarding data management, DG ECHO data maturity can be evaluated as “Established”. DG
ECHO will further develop its data warehouse and associated reporting tools. Special attention
will be given to the data preservation and deletion strategy. DG ECHO will continue to deliver
tailored training and organise awareness-raising activities for DG ECHO staff. DG ECHO will
15

continue to update its dedicated 'DG ECHO Data Protection Corner' page. Quarterly awareness-
raising sessions will be held, and open to all DG ECHO staff (HQ and Field). DG ECHO will
review Data Protection Records subject to biennial review while having new processing
operations being covered by new Data Protection Records. DG ECHO will also continue
collaborating to the Global Europe family network on data maturity and governance to further
develop its data maturity. Through this group, best practices are promoted and common actions
are developed. For example, specific attention will be given to the design of training paths for
data stewards/owners, to the pilot of DG DIGIT for testing the self- assessment tool on data
quality.
As a follow-up to the implementing activities carried out so far, DG ECHO will continue adapting
its privacy statements to the related decentralised corporate records for common processing
operations within the Commission’s services, as well as mapping the data processing activities
by proactively reaching out to operational controllers.
Knowledge management on Civil Protection will continue to be a priority within ECHO and with
the external stakeholders of the European Civil Protection community.
C. Sound financial management
DG ECHO’s internal control system ensures an adequate management of the risks related to
the legality and regularity of underlying transactions, while taking into account the nature of
the payments concerned. In 2026, the main financial control objective remains to ensure that
the residual error rate does not exceed the materiality threshold of 2%. For complex multi-
beneficiary Humanitarian Aid grants and Programmatic Partnership projects, and beneficiary
grants with Partners identified as having a high error rate (>2%), Certified Financial Statements
are requested above EUR 325.000 per partner at execution. Other indicators used to ensure
sound financial management are the average time to pay, and the percentage of amounts paid
within the legal time. DG ECHO will strive to achieve an adequate balance between the controls
carried out and the related costs, aiming to keep the cost of controls under the ceiling of 0.5%
of the total of funds controlled, as targeted in Annex 2.
Due to the different financial procedures and risk profiles of DG ECHO’s activities, separate
control systems are in place for humanitarian and civil protection actions implemented under
indirect and direct management. For humanitarian aid funds, the EU Humanitarian Partnership
Certificate, will continue to provide DG ECHO with assurance of the adequacy of the
management and control systems of INGOs implementing direct management funds. For
indirect management, assurance is provided by the Pillar Assessment and the controls
performed on reports or management declarations received from the entities implementing DG
ECHO’s funds. Civil Protection grants are managed through eGrants.
DG ECHO aims to monitor the implementation of all CP and HUMA grants, with on-the-spot
visits despite access, security restrictions or other constraints faced in humanitarian contexts.
Ex post controls are carried out according to the annual audit plans which provide final
assurance to the authorising officer by sub- delegation that payments done are legal and
regular. The annual audit plan sets out ex- post controls on the different types of actions
16

funded, as well as on control systems of partners to verify the legality and regularity of the
selected transactions and the adequacy of partners’ control systems.
D. Fraud risk management
Based on the results of the IAS audit on the anti-fraud strategy and following a thorough and
bottom-up fraud risk assessment in line with the OLAF methodology, DG ECHO has finalised its
anti-fraud strategy for 2025-2028 on 24 July 2025. It includes an action plan that responds to
the main risks identified in this exercise and defines actions for 2026, which include but are not
limited to enhanced outreach and awareness. Awareness sessions will be held in 2026 as
detailed in Annex 2. DG ECHO will continue cooperating with OLAF on the implementation of the
Commission Anti-Fraud Strategy and the related Action Plan and actively contribute to the
drafting of the new CAFS and its Action Plan by participating in the announced consultations.
Regarding protection from sexual exploitation, abuse and harassment (PSEAH), the DG ECHO
strategy will be further implemented in 2026 and the PSEAH package further disseminated. DG
ECHO will continue to request its partners to report annually on allegations of sexual
exploitation, abuse and harassment (SEAH) and to inform immediately on critically sensitive
cases. DG ECHO continues treating allegations from whistle-blowers as well as critically
sensitive allegations.
Concerning aid diversion, in line with its guidelines published in December 2024, DG ECHO will
reach out to its partner organisations to reinforce their capacities and systems to better detect,
prevent and address aid diversion. DG ECHO will also continue to engage with other donors to
raise attention to this issue.
E. Sound environmental management
The European Commission aims to be climate neutral by 2030. In 2026, DG ECHO will
contribute to this goal, complying with EMAS requirements by reducing travel emissions and
improving waste management, reducing energy consumption by following Belgian EPB
recommendations and implementing green tips for computer and light use, as well as adjusting
heating and air conditioning, while recognising that due to DG ECHO and ERCC’s core activities,
the complete closing of DG ECHO’s buildings during the end of the year and in summer is not
possible (but Loi 102 will continue to be closed at these moments).
In order to reduce by 50% in 2030, the 913.4 CO2 tonnes (based on data for the year 2019)
produced annually by professional travel, DG ECHO will promote eco-friendly travel by
encouraging staff to use soft mobility and public transport and by prioritising virtual meetings
whilst still ensuring accountability in all DG ECHO’s operations. In 2026 DG ECHO will Increase
green public procurement by introducing environmental criteria for products and services.
Further, DG ECHO will promote digital sobriety by raising awareness about the energy
consumption of digital tools. Additionally, we will promote eco-friendly practices in the digital
sphere, such as paperless operations and raise awareness about the energy consumption of AI
prompts, supporting the Commission's IT greening efforts; and increase staff engagement by
promoting participation in EMAS campaigns and activities.
